title: 5G Awareness and its Link to COVID-19: Case of Zambians with Access to Internet
screen_reason: Online self-administered survey of 258 internet-using Zambians (June-July 2020). One item asks directly whether the respondent has ever HEARD the false claim that COVID-19 symptoms are connected to 5G mobile-network radiation; 162/258 (62.9%) said yes. That is a share of respondents reporting encounter with a specific piece of misinformation, i.e. RECALL exposure, and it is reported with an explicit numerator and denominator in Table 1. Everything else in the paper is belief/opinion (14% believed the 5G claim, 57% think the virus was laboratory-created, 47% think the pandemic was planned, 21% think COVID-19 is a hoax, 11% think the virus travels over 5G), which the protocol excludes, plus a technical review of 5G radio-frequency health research.

estimates.platform: Online self-administered questionnaire (Google Forms) distributed via Facebook and WhatsApp groups; the claim itself circulated on social media
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported ever having heard the (false) claim that COVID-19 symptoms are connected to 5G mobile-network radiation
estimates.value_raw: 162/258 = 62.9% answered YES ('Have you ever heard that symptoms of COVID-19 seem to be connected to 5G mobile network'); NO 72 (27.8%), Not Sure 24 (9.3%)
estimates.denominator: 258 Zambian internet users who completed the online questionnaire (71.1% male; 53% aged 21-30)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'Yes' to having ever heard information linking COVID-19 symptoms to 5G mobile technology radiation
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper does not define misinformation formally; it treats the 5G-COVID-19 link as a conspiracy theory contradicted by evidence - “there have been conspiracy theories that were circulating on social media platforms perpetuating that radiation from 5G towers are linked to symptoms associated with COVID-19” and “Results also shows that there is no link between 5G and COVID-19 as far as health issues are concerned.”
estimates.source_quote: Have you ever heard that symptoms of COVID-19 seem to be connected to 5G mobile network | 258 | 162 | 62.9 | 72 | 27.8 | 24 | 9.3 (Table 1). Text: "On the question that asked if respondents have heard information linking symptoms of COVID-19 to 5G mobile technology radiation, 63% agreed they have heard such information. 28% had not heard the information and 9% were not sure."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The single target claim was designated false by the authors on the basis of the scientific literature they review (no consistent evidence of RF-EMF health effects in the 5G band; scientific consensus that SARS-CoV-2 has a natural origin). No fact-checker, no coding of respondent-supplied content, no reliability statistic - the falsity judgment is the authors' and applies to one pre-specified claim.
estimates.moderator_quote: The population of respondents came from members of the public with access to Internet. ... Random sampling was used to administer online questionnaire using Google Forms. The survey link was shared on Facebook and various WhatsApp groups to get wide range of respondents.
estimates.notes: The value itself is unambiguous (Table 1 gives the counts; the abstract rounds to 'about 62%' and the results text to '63%'). Generalisability is weak: the frame is Zambians with internet access (9.1 million mobile-broadband users, 2.3 million social-media users), the sample is 258 people recruited by posting a link to Facebook and WhatsApp groups, and it is 71.1% male and heavily skewed to ages 21-30. The paper calls this 'random sampling' and cites a Cochran minimum of 249, but a link shared into social-media groups is a convenience/self-selected sample, so sampling_frame is coded convenience rather than survey_sample. No response rate can be computed. This is exposure to ONE specific claim, not to misinformation in general, so it is not comparable with generic 'have you seen false information' items.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) All belief items - 14% believed the 5G-COVID claim, 57% think the virus was created in a laboratory, 47% think the pandemic was planned by pharmaceutical corporations and governments to depopulate the world, 25% think the dangers of coronavirus are covered up by the telecoms industry, 21% think COVID-19 is a hoax, 11% think the virus can be transmitted through 5G - belief in false claims is explicitly outside the review's scope. (b) 43% saying there is no good reason for the lockdown - a policy opinion, not a veracity judgment. (c) Source-of-information shares (78% social media, 61% internet, 52% TV, 29% newspapers) and 5G-awareness shares (67% aware of 5G, 30% aware of the reserved frequency bands) - media use and technology awareness, not misinformation exposure. (d) '37% of respondents' from a UK survey of 949 people, cited in the literature review - a figure from another study, barred by R8. (e) The cross-tabulations and chi-square/Fisher tests linking 5G awareness to conspiracy items are associations, not prevalence shares.

rob.design: Online self-administered questionnaire (21 items, Google Forms), June-July 2020, link distributed through Facebook and WhatsApp groups; frame = Zambian internet users (ZICTA: 9.1 million mobile-broadband users, 2.3 million social-media users). Cochran-formula minimum sample size 249; 258 responded. Self-selected sample, no response rate reportable, 71.1% male, 53% aged 21-30, 8.3% over 45. Single-item self-reported exposure to one pre-specified false claim; no coding of content and therefore no inter-rater reliability. Analysis is descriptive plus Pearson chi-square and Fisher exact tests.
